questions.stem: Two hours after thyroidectomy, a client reports increasing neck pressure and difficulty swallowing. The nurse notes new anterior neck swelling and a change in voice. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's priority response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect a postoperative neck hematoma with possible evolving airway compromise and escalate the assessment immediately rather than treating the symptoms as routine edema.","B":"Interpret the findings as expected postoperative tissue swelling and continue routine observation unless the oxygen saturation falls below the prescribed target.","C":"Attribute the symptoms primarily to transient recurrent-laryngeal-nerve irritation because a hematoma generally causes obvious external bleeding before pressure symptoms.","D":"Treat the swallowing difficulty as postoperative nausea and delay focused airway assessment until analgesia and antiemetic therapy have had time to take effect."}}
questions.rationale: Neck swelling, dysphagia, voice change, and respiratory findings after thyroidectomy can indicate hemorrhage or swelling that threatens the airway. Early focused airway assessment and escalation are required.
questions.source_detail: Post-thyroidectomy airway compromise may result from hemorrhage or swelling; warning signs include neck swelling, difficulty breathing or swallowing, stridor, and oxygenation changes.

questions.stem: Several hours after cranial surgery, a client becomes progressively drowsy, vomits, develops new unilateral weakness, and has unequal pupils. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are expected residual effects of anesthesia and can be trended until the next scheduled neurological assessment if vital signs remain stable.","B":"The findings most likely reflect uncomplicated postoperative pain because vomiting and pupillary asymmetry commonly occur during routine recovery.","C":"The findings suggest acute neurological deterioration with possible intracranial hypertension or herniation and require urgent neurocritical reassessment.","D":"The findings primarily indicate dehydration from perioperative fasting and should be reassessed after oral fluids are offered and tolerated."}}
questions.rationale: Progressive reduction in consciousness, vomiting, new focal deficit, and pupillary asymmetry are acute neurological warning signs. ENLS includes recognition and staged management of intracranial hypertension and cerebral herniation.
questions.source_name: Neurocritical Care Society — Emergency Neurological Life Support (ENLS) 6.0
questions.source_detail: Current ENLS 6.0 includes modules on the comatose patient and intracranial hypertension/herniation with objectives to recognize signs and initiate staged emergency management.

questions.stem: A medically stable hospitalized client reports sleeping only a few hours each night because of hallway noise, bright lights, routine overnight interruptions, and nonurgent care. Which nursing plan is best?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Request a sedative-hypnotic as the first intervention and maintain the usual overnight care schedule because environmental changes have limited effect on hospital sleep.","B":"Cluster nonurgent care when clinically safe, reduce avoidable noise and light, and coordinate routine nighttime tasks well to limit unnecessary sleep disruption.","C":"Keep the room brightly lit overnight to preserve orientation and schedule hourly checks even when not clinically required, because monitoring should take priority over sleep.","D":"Encourage long daytime naps and evening caffeine so the client can compensate for nighttime interruptions while leaving the unit's nighttime routine unchanged."}}
questions.rationale: Hospital sleep disruption is commonly worsened by noise, bright light, and unnecessary nighttime staff activity. Nonpharmacologic environmental and workflow changes should be used when clinically safe before reflexively adding sedatives.
questions.source_name: AHRQ PSNet — Good Night's Sleep Gone Wrong
questions.source_detail: AHRQ PSNet describes hospital sleep protocols that reduce noise and light and limit avoidable nighttime medications, procedures, laboratory draws, and staff disruptions.
